passage:
Monday. Kavitha's cat, Pepper, had been missing for four days. Every night Kavitha lit a lamp in the puja room and prayed with her whole heart: please bring Pepper home.
Friday. The neighbour found Pepper's collar near the main road, but not Pepper. Kavitha stopped lighting the lamp. At night she lay awake with a strange, hollow question: is anyone even listening? It felt wicked to think it. She didn't tell anyone.
Sunday. Manoj Mama came to visit and found her sitting alone on the steps. When she finally whispered her question, he didn't look shocked. 'I've asked that too,' he said. 'Many good people have. Asking isn't wicked. Let's talk about it whenever you want.' Kavitha leaned against his arm and cried for Pepper properly.

qa.q: What did the neighbour find near the main road?
qa.a: Pepper's collar.

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling as she lay awake on Friday night?
qa.a: Hollow and confused, wondering if anyone was listening, and ashamed, as if the question were wicked.

qa.q: What helped Kavitha with her doubt?
qa.a: Telling Manoj Mama, who said asking isn't wicked and offered to talk whenever she wanted.

qa.q: How did Manoj Mama respond to Kavitha's question?
qa.a: Calmly and honestly; he admitted he had asked it too.

grounding: Over a week a girl whose prayer for her lost cat goes unanswered begins to doubt, and talks to a trusted uncle instead of hiding it.

passage: 'Gautam, you think God didn't hear you because you lost the chess final? Let your Anand Dadu tell you something. When I was ten, the rains failed in our village. I prayed every morning at the little Shiva shrine by the well: please, rain. I even gave up sweets. No rain came. Our wheat dried out. I remember sitting on the dry field, angry and scared, thinking maybe nobody was up there at all. I felt so guilty for thinking it that I hid from the temple for weeks. Then the old pujari found me and asked why. I told the truth. The pujari laughed gently and said, "Even the sages asked that, child. Doubt is only honest thinking. Bring it to me whenever you like." I did, for years.'

qa.q: What did young Anand give up while praying for rain?
qa.a: Sweets.

qa.q: What was young Anand feeling on the dry field?
qa.a: Angry and scared, doubting anyone was up there, and then guilty for thinking it.

qa.q: What choice in the story helped Anand with his doubt?
qa.a: Telling the old pujari honestly instead of hiding, and bringing Anand's questions there for years.

qa.q: How did the old pujari see Anand's doubt?
qa.a: As honest thinking, something even sages asked, not something wicked.

grounding: A grandfather recalls doubting when his prayers for rain went unanswered, and bringing the doubt to a trusted elder.

passage: In Lagos, Christmas Eve had Emeka bouncing off the walls. Mum's jollof rice was bubbling, his new shirt with gold buttons hung on the door, and cousins were arriving from Enugu. He couldn't stop grinning. Then, through the window, he saw the girl from the flat opposite, Yuki, sitting alone on her steps. Her family had moved from Osaka a month ago, and she had told him her parents would be working at the port over Christmas. Emeka stopped bouncing. He went to the kitchen. 'Mum, can Yuki come for rice? She's by herself.' Mum wiped her hands. 'Go and ask her. And take her a plate of chin chin now.' Yuki's face, when he held out the plate, made his Christmas even brighter.

qa.q: Where had Yuki's family moved from?
qa.a: Osaka.

qa.q: How was Emeka feeling on Christmas Eve before he saw Yuki?
qa.a: Bubbling with excitement; he was bouncing off the walls and couldn't stop grinning 🎉

qa.q: How did Emeka share his joy?
qa.a: He noticed Yuki alone, asked Mum if she could come for rice, and took her a plate of chin chin.

qa.q: How might Yuki have felt when Emeka held out the plate?
qa.a: Surprised and warmed, and less alone while her parents worked.

grounding: A boy bubbling with Christmas excitement notices a neighbour who cannot celebrate with family and shares with her.

passage: In the boarding school dining hall, everyone was buzzing: Diwali holidays started tomorrow. Avni had packed three days ago. Her new lehenga was folded on top, and Mummy had promised kaju katli and a house full of cousins. She was practically floating. At dinner she noticed Zubin, from her class, pushing peas around his plate. His parents were working in Dubai, and he was staying at the hostel for the holidays with the warden. Avni's floating feeling wobbled. She thought for a moment, then took out the packet of sweets and the box of sparklers she'd been saving for the train. 'For you. Light them with the warden on Diwali night, and I'll light mine at the same time.' Zubin looked up and smiled for the first time all week.

qa.q: Where were Zubin's parents working?
qa.a: In Dubai.

qa.q: What was Avni feeling before dinner, and how did it change?
qa.a: Excited and floating at first; it wobbled into concern when she saw Zubin alone.

qa.q: How did Avni share her festival joy?
qa.a: She gave Zubin her sweets and sparklers and planned to light hers at the same time.

qa.q: What was it like for Zubin at dinner before Avni spoke?
qa.a: Lonely and low, pushing peas around his plate while everyone else was going home.

grounding: At a boarding school a girl excited about going home for Diwali remembers a classmate who cannot, and shares with him.

passage: At the Ganesh festival in our building compound last year, the older kids were taking turns to carry the small palki. I'm Mohit. When I stepped up, one of the organisers looked at the surname on my name tag and said, 'Not you. This is only for our people.' I didn't even understand what he meant. My face went hot, and I stood at the back, confused, trying not to cry. I told Lakshmi Aunty from the second floor, who was running the prasad table. She put down her ladle, took my hand and walked straight to the organiser. 'Every child here can carry it,' she said firmly. The pujari nodded. 'God does not shut out children.' I carried the palki in the next round. Aunty told me it was never my fault.

qa.q: What was Mohit told at the palki?
qa.a: 'Not you. This is only for our people.'

qa.q: How did Mohit feel standing at the back?
qa.a: Hurt and confused, face hot, trying not to cry.

qa.q: What did Mohit do, and how did the adult respond?
qa.a: Told Lakshmi Aunty, who went straight to the organiser, said every child can carry the palki, and told Mohit it was never Mohit's fault.

qa.q: How did the pujari see the organiser's rule?
qa.a: As wrong; the pujari said God does not shut out children.

grounding: A child shut out of a festival ritual because of their family name tells a trusted adult, who restores their place at once.

passage:
Note by Tanuja D'Costa, Sunday school coordinator, after the Christmas party.
Vidya, aged nine, came with her neighbours, the Fernandes family. When the children lined up for the nativity play, one of our volunteers told her, 'You can't be in it. You're not one of us.' I saw Vidya's face crumple; she went and sat under the stairs, hugging her knees. Mrs Fernandes found her and brought her to me straight away. I knelt beside Vidya and told her clearly that it was not her fault and that no child is shut out here. I gave her the part of a star, and she shone at it, holding up her tinsel. I have spoken to the volunteer, and this evening I phoned Vidya's mother to explain and apologise.

qa.q: Where did Vidya go after being told she couldn't join?
qa.a: Under the stairs, hugging her knees.

qa.q: What did Vidya's crumpling face show?
qa.a: She felt hurt and confused at being shut out.

qa.q: What did the coordinator do the same day?
qa.a: Told Vidya it wasn't her fault, gave her the star part, spoke to the volunteer and phoned her mother to apologise.

qa.q: How might Mrs Fernandes have felt finding Vidya under the stairs?
qa.a: Upset and protective, which is why she brought Vidya to the coordinator straight away.

grounding: A coordinator's note records a visiting girl told she cannot join a church play, and adults at once including her and correcting the volunteer.

passage:
'Parveen, you're not eating again?' Deepika held out her tiffin. 'Take a paratha.'
'Thanks, but I'm fasting. It's Ramzan.'
Deepika tilted her head. 'The whole day? Not even water?'
'Not even water, till sunset.'
'Can I ask why? I'm not being rude. I really want to know.'
Parveen smiled. 'It's to remember people who don't have enough, and to feel close to God. And to practise patience. My Ammi says it makes you kinder.'
'Doesn't your stomach growl in maths?'
'Loudly.' They both laughed.
'So what do you eat at sunset?'
'Dates first. Then everything! Want to come for iftar on Friday? Ammi makes the best pakoras.'
Deepika grinned. 'I'll ask Mummy. And I won't eat my tiffin in front of you today.'
'You can. It's fine. But thanks.'

qa.q: What does Parveen eat first at sunset?
qa.a: Dates.

qa.q: Why did Deepika say 'I'm not being rude'?
qa.a: Deepika felt curious but careful, wanting to understand the fast respectfully without upsetting Parveen.

qa.q: What did Deepika do that showed respect?
qa.a: Asked kindly, listened to the reasons, and offered not to eat the tiffin in front of Parveen.

qa.q: How did Parveen feel about Deepika's questions?
qa.a: Pleased and open; Parveen smiled, explained, laughed along and invited Deepika for iftar 🙂

grounding: A child curious about a friend's fast asks kindly and listens, learning a different practice can be sincere.

passage: In Class 5, I noticed that my friend Usha always touched the small silver cross on her chain before tests. I'm Arnab. I was curious, but also shy, because I didn't want to sound silly. One day, sharing a bench in the library, I asked, 'Why do you touch it before tests?' Usha thought for a bit. 'It reminds me I'm not alone. My grandmother gave it to me.' I told her that I say a small prayer to Saraswati before exams, and that my Dida gave me a red thread for my wrist. We compared: her cross, my thread. Both from grandmothers. Both meaning 'you're not alone'. I walked home thinking that different ways could be equally sincere, and that asking had been easy after all.

qa.q: Who gave Usha the cross?
qa.a: Her grandmother.

qa.q: How did Arnab feel before asking about the cross?
qa.a: Curious but shy, worried about sounding silly.

qa.q: What did Arnab gain by asking kindly?
qa.a: Arnab learned the cross reminds Usha she's not alone, and saw it was like Arnab's own red thread, equally sincere.

qa.q: How did Usha respond to Arnab's question?
qa.a: Thoughtfully and openly; she explained what it meant to her.

grounding: A child curious about a friend's cross asks kindly, listens, and sees that different ways can each be sincere.

passage: The parish hall in Pune glowed with paper stars, and Darshan hovered at the door, unsure where to stand. Francis, beaming under his new haircut, grabbed his arm. 'You came! Come and sit with my family.' During the service Francis whispered explanations: 'That's the crib, with baby Jesus. Now everyone stands. You don't have to sing if you don't know it.' Darshan stood when they stood and folded his hands the way he did at home. When people went up for communion, Francis said, 'That part is only for us. Stay here with Mummy, she'll keep you company.' Afterwards, over plum cake, Darshan said, 'It's different from our Ganpati puja, but the feeling of everyone together is the same.' Francis's mother smiled. 'Come every year.'

qa.q: What did the parish hall glow with?
qa.a: Paper stars.

qa.q: How did Darshan feel as Francis explained things?
qa.a: Welcomed and more at ease after hovering unsure at the door.

qa.q: How did Darshan join respectfully?
qa.a: He stood when others stood, folded his hands as he did at home, and stayed back during communion, without needing to share every belief.

qa.q: How did Francis's mother see Darshan's visit?
qa.a: Warmly; she smiled and invited him to come every year.

grounding: A boy invited to his friend's Christmas service feels welcome as the friend explains, and joins respectfully without needing to agree.

passage:
Thursday. Thomas handed Bidisha an envelope with a hand-drawn egg on it. 'Easter lunch at our place, Sunday. Amma says you have to come.' Bidisha felt a flutter: she had never been to an Easter anything.
Sunday. Thomas met her at the gate and explained everything patiently. 'We went to church this morning, that's why Appachan is still in his white shirt. The eggs are for new life. Want to help hide them for the little ones?' At lunch his grandmother said a short prayer. Bidisha bowed her head politely and didn't pretend to say the words. Nobody minded. She felt welcome all the way through the appam and stew.
Monday. Bidisha told Ma, 'Their prayers are different from ours. But I didn't feel I had to change anything. I just felt invited.'

qa.q: What was drawn on Thomas's envelope?
qa.a: An egg.

qa.q: How did Bidisha feel at Thomas's Easter lunch?
qa.a: Welcome and comfortable, all the way through the appam and stew.

qa.q: How did Bidisha join respectfully?
qa.a: She helped hide the eggs and bowed her head politely during the prayer without pretending to say words she didn't share.

qa.q: How did Thomas make Bidisha feel included?
qa.a: He explained each thing patiently and gave her a job hiding eggs.

grounding: Over several days a girl invited to her friend's Easter lunch feels welcome and joins respectfully without feeling her own faith is threatened.

passage:
Thursday
Diary, it's Suraj. Today during break, some boys snatched Irfan's white prayer cap and passed it round, putting it on their heads and pulling faces. Everyone was laughing, so I laughed too. Loudly. Irfan stood there trying to smile, but his ears were red, and he kept holding out his hand for it. When he finally got it back, he folded it very carefully into his bag, as if it were hurt. I felt sick in my stomach all through maths. I didn't even think it was funny. I laughed because I didn't want them laughing at me. Tomorrow, if they start again, I'm going to walk away, or say 'Let's go and play cricket' instead. I'm going to tell Irfan sorry. And if they keep doing it, I'll tell Sir.

qa.q: What did the boys snatch from Irfan?
qa.a: His white prayer cap.

qa.q: How did Suraj feel during maths?
qa.a: Sick in the stomach and guilty, knowing the laughing hurt Irfan and wasn't even funny.

qa.q: What braver choices does Suraj plan?
qa.a: Walking away or suggesting cricket if it starts again, apologising to Irfan, and telling Sir if it continues.

qa.q: How did Irfan feel while his cap was passed around?
qa.a: Hurt and humiliated; his ears were red and he tried to smile while holding out his hand.

grounding: A child who laughed along at a classmate's prayer cap to fit in feels sick about it and plans to step aside and apologise.

passage: In the village school near Malda, the girls ate lunch on the verandah. When Ayesha unrolled her small prayer mat in a corner of the empty classroom, Rupa peeked in and giggled, 'Look, she's doing exercise!' The others laughed and started copying her bowing. Usha laughed too. It felt good to be part of the loud group. Then she saw Ayesha's shoulders go stiff through the window, and her own laugh stuck in her throat. Ayesha had shared her guavas with Usha only yesterday. The next day, when Rupa said, 'Let's go and watch her pray,' Usha said, 'Let's play hopscotch instead,' and walked towards the chalk squares. Two girls followed her. At the end of lunch, Usha sat next to Ayesha and offered her a piece of roti.

qa.q: What did Ayesha unroll in the empty classroom?
qa.a: Her small prayer mat.

qa.q: Why did Usha's laugh stick in her throat?
qa.a: She felt guilty and ashamed when she saw Ayesha's shoulders go stiff, remembering Ayesha had shared guavas with her.

qa.q: What braver choice did Usha make the next day?
qa.a: She suggested hopscotch instead of watching Ayesha pray, walked away from the teasing, and sat with Ayesha.

qa.q: How might Ayesha have felt when the girls copied her bowing?
qa.a: Hurt and embarrassed; her shoulders went stiff.

grounding: A village girl who laughed along at a classmate's prayers to fit in feels ashamed and changes the subject the next day.

passage: Every Tuesday, my Nani puts a small red tilak on my forehead after her puja, before school. I'm Sunaina. Last year, at a new school, a group of boys started calling me 'Dot' and poking their own foreheads when I walked by. By the third Tuesday, I scrubbed the tilak off in the school washroom until my skin went pink. I felt ashamed of Nani's puja, and that made me feel even worse. My friend Nitin saw my red forehead and said, 'You have to tell Ma'am. Today.' He came with me. Ma'am listened, then told the boys that making fun of anyone's faith is not allowed in her class. That evening I told Nani too. She hugged me and said, 'Who you are is nothing to hide.' I wear it again now.

qa.q: What did the boys call Sunaina?
qa.a: 'Dot'.

qa.q: How did Sunaina feel scrubbing off the tilak?
qa.a: Ashamed and hurt, and even worse for feeling ashamed of Nani's puja.

qa.q: What helped Sunaina?
qa.a: Nitin urging Sunaina to tell Ma'am that day and going along, Ma'am stopping the boys, and Nani's hug and words that evening.

qa.q: How might Nani have felt hearing about the teasing?
qa.a: Sad and protective; she hugged Sunaina and said who Sunaina is is nothing to hide.

grounding: A child mocked for a faith mark feels ashamed, tells a teacher the same day with a friend's help, and is supported by family.

passage:
Class 4 teacher's note, by Joseph Mathew, Wednesday.
During PT, I saw three children pulling at the patka on Jagdish's head and chanting, 'Pineapple head!' Jagdish was trying to hold it on with both hands, blinking fast. I stopped the game at once and took the three children to one side. I told them firmly that mocking anyone's faith or dress is never acceptable here, and that they will apologise to him tomorrow in front of me. Then I sat with Jagdish on the steps. He said quietly, 'Maybe I should stop wearing it.' I told him his patka and his faith are nothing to be ashamed of, and that the fault was theirs, not his. I have informed the principal and phoned his parents; his father will come in tomorrow.

qa.q: What did the children chant at Jagdish?
qa.a: 'Pineapple head!'

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling when he said 'Maybe I should stop wearing it'?
qa.a: Ashamed and hurt enough to think of hiding part of who he is.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that same day?
qa.a: Stopped the game, spoke firmly to the three children, reassured Jagdish, and informed the principal and his parents.

qa.q: How might Jagdish's father feel coming in tomorrow?
qa.a: Upset and protective, wanting his son to feel safe at school.

grounding: A teacher's note records a boy mocked for his patka, the teacher's same-day response, and reassurance that nothing is wrong with his faith.

passage:
'Who were you playing with downstairs?' Parul Bua asked.
'Salim. From the third floor. He's my best friend.'
Bua's mouth tightened. 'Stay away from those people. They're not like us. They're bad.'
Omkar's stomach went funny. 'But... Salim shared his lunch with me every day when I broke my arm. And his Ammi fixed my kite.'
'That's how they fool you.'
Omkar looked at the floor. He didn't want to be rude to Bua. 'Bua, which people are bad? All of them? Have you met Salim?'
Bua opened her mouth, then closed it. 'Well. No.'
'Can I bring him to say hello tomorrow?'
Bua sniffed. 'We'll see.'
That night Omkar asked Papa, who said quietly, 'Judge people by what they do, beta. You know Salim.'

qa.q: What did Salim's Ammi fix for Omkar?
qa.a: His kite.

qa.q: Why did Omkar's stomach go funny?
qa.a: He felt confused and uneasy, because Bua called Salim's people bad while Salim had been so kind.

qa.q: How did Omkar stay polite while holding on to what he knew?
qa.a: He shared his own experience of Salim and asked calm questions instead of arguing rudely.

qa.q: What might Bua have felt when Omkar asked if she had met Salim?
qa.a: Caught off guard and perhaps a little unsure, since she had to admit she hadn't.

grounding: A boy confused when an aunt calls his friend's community bad holds on to his own experience and asks calm questions.

passage: When I was nine, my best friend Noor sent a box of sheer khurma to our house on Eid. I'm Keerthana. My Paati looked at the box and said, 'Don't eat that. Those people are not good.' I stood there holding the box, my face hot and my head spinning. Noor had held my hand on my first day of school. How could Noor be 'not good'? I didn't shout at Paati; she's my Paati and I love her. Instead I asked, 'Paati, what did they do?' She couldn't really say. Later I asked Amma, who said, 'You know Noor. Trust what you have seen.' A month later, Noor came over for Pongal and helped Paati stir the pot. Paati didn't say anything. But she gave Noor the first taste.

qa.q: What did Noor send on Eid?
qa.a: A box of sheer khurma.

qa.q: How did Keerthana feel when Paati called Noor's family not good?
qa.a: Confused and upset, face hot and head spinning, because Noor had always been kind.

qa.q: How did Keerthana respond without being rude to Paati?
qa.a: Keerthana calmly asked Paati what they had done and took Amma's advice to trust what had actually been seen.

qa.q: What might Paati giving Noor the first taste show?
qa.a: That meeting Noor may have begun to soften Paati's view.

grounding: A child confused by a grandmother's prejudice against a friend's faith holds on to experience and asks questions without rudeness.

passage:
Football coach's note, by Ramesh Nair, Saturday practice.
During the water break, one of the older boys laughed at the prayer beads Tenzin wears on his wrist and said his religion was 'just weird chanting'. A few others smirked. Tenzin went quiet and pulled his sleeve down. Before I could step in, Noor stood up. Her voice shook a little, but she said, 'Don't talk about his religion like that. Would you like it if someone said that about yours?' The older boy muttered something and walked off. I then spoke to him and the others myself: no mocking of anyone's faith on this team. Noor sat next to Tenzin for the rest of the break. Afterwards I told Noor that what she did took courage.

qa.q: What does Tenzin wear on his wrist?
qa.a: Prayer beads.

qa.q: What does Noor's shaking voice suggest?
qa.a: She was nervous and uncomfortable, but loyal enough to Tenzin to speak up anyway.

qa.q: What did the coach do after Noor spoke up?
qa.a: Spoke to the older boy and the others, saying no mocking of anyone's faith on the team, and praised Noor's courage.

qa.q: How might Tenzin have felt when Noor stood up for him?
qa.a: Relieved and supported after going quiet and hiding his beads.

grounding: A coach's note records a girl speaking up when a friend's religion is insulted, despite discomfort, and the coach backing her.

passage:
Monday
Dear diary, Dolma here. Today in the canteen, a boy from 6C saw the little Durga sticker on Anirban's lunch box and said, 'Ha, your goddess has ten arms, like an octopus. Your religion is a cartoon.' Everyone at the table laughed, and Anirban just stared at his rice. My heart was pounding so hard I thought everyone could hear it. I don't pray to Durga. But Anirban is my friend. So I said, 'Stop. You wouldn't like it if someone laughed at your prayers.' The boy rolled his eyes and said, 'Chill,' but he stopped. After lunch Anirban said, 'Thanks,' very quietly. I felt shaky for an hour. I'd rather feel shaky than be the person who said nothing. I also told Ma'am at the end of the day, and she said she'd speak to him.

qa.q: What sticker was on Anirban's lunch box?
qa.a: A little Durga sticker.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling while speaking up?
qa.a: Nervous and scared, heart pounding, yet loyal enough to Anirban to say something.

qa.q: What did Dolma do at the end of the day to follow up?
qa.a: Told Ma'am, who said she would speak to the boy.

qa.q: How did Anirban feel after Dolma spoke up?
qa.a: Grateful, though still shaken; he thanked Dolma very quietly.

grounding: A child speaks up when a friend's religion is mocked, despite feeling uncomfortable, and tells a teacher the same day.

passage: On Republic Day, the whole village school near Bareilly lined up in the dusty courtyard. When the sarpanch pulled the rope and the flag opened, petals fell out, and everyone sang the anthem. Asif stood so straight his back hurt. Goosebumps ran up his arms. He felt as if the whole country was standing with him. Afterwards the teachers handed out laddoos. Asif noticed a few children from the brick kiln watching from outside the fence, not in school uniform. Vidya noticed too. 'They sang the anthem as well,' she whispered. 'I heard them.' Asif looked at his laddoo, then walked to the fence and broke it in half. Vidya did the same. Then Masterji saw, and carried the whole tray over. It felt as good as the anthem.

qa.q: What fell out when the flag opened?
qa.a: Petals.

qa.q: How did Asif feel during the anthem?
qa.a: Proud and moved; goosebumps ran up his arms and he felt the whole country standing with him.

qa.q: How did Asif turn his pride into care?
qa.a: He shared his laddoo with the children from the brick kiln who had sung the anthem outside the fence.

qa.q: How might the brick-kiln children have felt at the fence?
qa.a: Surprised and included, since they had sung the anthem too.

grounding: A village boy feels deep pride at the Republic Day anthem and turns it into care for children outside the school fence.

passage: At Mei's school in Singapore, the National Day assembly began with the whole hall singing the anthem. Mei stood tall in her red T-shirt, and when the drums came in, goosebumps prickled her arms. She thought of her grandfather, who had come by boat long ago and helped build the flats she lived in. Afterwards, each class got goodie bags with flags and cold drinks. Through the window Mei saw the workers repainting the school fence in the heat, sweating in their helmets. 'They're building the country too,' she said to Santiago, the new boy from Chile. They asked their teacher, who helped the class carry a crate of cold drinks outside. One worker grinned and waved a tiny flag. Mei felt proud all over again, in a bigger way.

qa.q: What colour was Mei's T-shirt?
qa.a: Red.

qa.q: How did Mei feel when the drums came in?
qa.a: Proud and moved; goosebumps prickled her arms.

qa.q: How did Mei's pride grow into caring for others?
qa.a: She saw the workers repainting the fence as part of the country and, with her class and teacher, took them cold drinks.

qa.q: How might the worker who waved a flag have felt?
qa.a: Appreciated and included in the celebration.

grounding: A girl in Singapore feels pride during the anthem and extends it to caring for the workers who help build the country.
